Regioselective Hydro(deutero)silylation of 1,3-Enynes Enabled by
Photoredox/Nickel Dual Catalysis
Guodong Zhang,* Wei Tan, Duo Zhang,* Kaiping Wang, Pan Gao, Shuli Wang, Shuang-Liang Liu,
and Feng Chen*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 536−541
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: In the presence of visible light irradiation, organo-
photo/nickel dual catalysts, and the mild base K
2
HPO
4
, 1,3-enynes
react with silanecarboxylic acids to give the corresponding α-
silylallenes with high selectivity. In this uniquely decarboxylative
hydrosilylation of 1,3-enynes, a silyl radical process is involved and
diverse electron-rich and -poor substrates proceed smoothly in
moderate to excellent yields. This transformation is particularly
synthetically worthwhile when using MeOD as the solvent, which
furnishes new access to α-silyldeuteroallenes.
A
llene units not only widely exist in natural products,
pharmaceuticals, bioactive molecules, and functional
materials
1
but are also valuable intermediates in many organic
transformations.
2
The first example of allene synthesis could be
traced back to 1887 by Burton and Pechmann;
3
since then,
methods for the preparation of allenes have been well-
developed,
4
such as tropic rearrangement of propargylics,
5
prototropic isomerization of alkynes,
6
and elimination of
enolphosphates
7
or vinylsulfoxide.
8
However, limitations exist
with such approaches, which always rely on harsh reaction
conditions or tedious prefunctionalization of substrates, thus
greatly restricting their widespread applications. The nucleo-
philic addition of 1,3-enynes provides another way to allene
moieties (Scheme 1a).
9
Nevertheless, the use of highly active
and unstable organometallic reagents also hampers the
substrate scope.
With the rapid growth of photo- and electrocatalytic
synthesis in the past decade,
10
free radical chemistry has
achieved remarkable progress, which thus has brought the
radical addition of 1,3-enynes up to a new level. Peculiarly in
combination with transition-metal catalysis, a variety of 1,4-
difunctionalizations of 1,3-enynes have been successfully
implemented (Scheme 1b).
11
However, thus far established
radical precursors are primarily limited to alkyl,
12
perfluor-
oalkyl,
13
trifluoromethyl,
14
and sulfonyl
15
radical sources.
Other types of radical addition have been rarely studied, but
at all events, their development is a very appealing research
aspect to lead the radical addition reaction of 1,3-enynes into
synthetic maturity.
On the other hand, the introduction of silicon atoms can
improve the lipophilicity of organic molecules, modify their
physicochemical properties, particularly enhance the tissue
permeability of drugs, and prolong their action time. Thus,
silicon substitution plays an important role in the innovation
and development of new drugs.
16
Moreover, organosilicons
represent a class of irreplaceable synthons in numerous
classical reactions.
17
Therefore, selective installation of
complex organosilicon molecules has become a promising
area.
18
In recent years, the rise of photoinduced silyl radical

chemistry has provided a sustainable and efficient protocol for
C−Si bond formation. Initially, silyl radicals were generated
through the cleavage of Si−X (X = Hg, Se, B, P, Si, etc.) bonds
under ultraviolet (UV) irradiation.
19
However, such high-
energy irradiation inevitably causes the formation of undesired
byproducts. Direct activation of Si−H bonds under visible light
irradiation to produce silyl radicals always requires additionally
an expensive hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) catalyst.
20
Thus
indisputably, silanecarboxylic acids are ideal silyl radical
reagents that are easily available, highly stable, and easy to
operate. Moreover, their chemical properties are analogous to
those of carboxylic acids, where radical decarboxylation readily
occurs under mild and concise conditions. Heretofore,
decarboxylative fictionalizations of silanecarboxylic acids have
been scarcely studied, and only several examples, such as
alkylation,
21
allylation,
22
difluoroallylation,
23
and heterocyclic
arylation,
24
were documented. Intrigued by this, we report a
regioselective hydrosilylation of 1,3-enynes with silanecarbox-
ylic acids as the silylating sources. This reactivity is especially
synthetically useful when performed under MeOD as the
solvent, where deuterosilylation products were obtained with
high deuterium isotopic contents.
Our optimization was initiated by the use of (3-methylbut-3-
en-1-yn-1-yl)benzene (1a) and tert-butyldiphenylsilanecarbox-
ylic acid (2a) as the model reaction. Screening of catalysts
showed that the dual catalytic system with Ni(DME)Br
2
and
2,4,5,6-tetra(9H-carbazol-9-yl)isophthalonitrile (4CzIPN) fur-
nished the desired hydrosilylation product in 58% yield
(Tables S1 and S2 of the Supporting Information). Different
solvents were tested, among which originally used MeOH led
to a higher yield than the others (entries 1−6 in Table 1).
Switching the base from K
2
HPO
4
to K
2
CO
3
, K
3
PO
4
, or KOAc
gave inferior yields, indicating that K
2
HPO
4
was the most
powerful for this conversion (entries 7−9 in Table 1). A
further ligand evaluation suggested that the efficiency of dtbpy
(L1) was higher than that of other ligands (entries 10−17 in
Table 1). Only an 18% yield was detected in the absence of a
nickel catalyst (entry 18 in Table 1). To our delight, the yield
could be improved to 83% by increasing the loading of
compound 2a (entry 19 in Table 1). A control experiment
pointed out that photoirradiation is indispensable (entry 20 in
Table 1).
Under the optimized reaction conditions, the scope of 1,3-
enynes with compound 2a as the coupling partner was
evaluated (Table 2). The reactivity showed good functional
group tolerance. For instance, both electron-donating groups,
such as methyl, n-propyl, tert-butyl, and phenyl groups, and
electron-withdrawing groups, such as methoxycarbonyl,
trifluoromethyl, cyano groups, and halogen, were well-
compatible (3aa−3ma). 4-Alkyl-substituted 1,3-enyne was
suitable but resulted in an inferior yield (3na). Only a 26%
yield was obtained from internal 1,3-enyne (3oa), implying
that the reactivity of internal 1,3-enyne is lower than that of
terminal substrates. 2-Aryl-substituted 1,3-enyne was also
investigated. To our satisfaction, the target product was
delivered in a moderate yield (3pa). Subsequently, several
silanecarboxylic acids were explored to prove the widespread
applicability of this transformation. It was found that
methyldiphenylsilanecarboxylic acid proceeded smoothly and
led to the desired product efficiently (3ab). However,
methyldiphenylsilanecarboxylic acids with a methyl or tert-
butyl group at the meta or para position of the benzene ring
exhibited low reactivity (3ac−3ae). Note that methyldiphe-
nylsilanecarboxylic acid bearing a methyl group at the ortho
position of the benzene ring was inapplicable to this
conversion, probably as a result of high steric hindrance.
Dimethylphenylsilanecarboxylic acid and triphenylsilanecar-
boxylic acid also showed inefficiency under the current
catalytic system.
An infinitely better application of this transformation in
organic synthesis is that it can be used for assembling α-
silyldeuteroallenes. Amazingly, the deuterosilylation of 1,3-
enynes could proceed smoothly just by switching the solvent to
MeOD, leading to good yields as well as high deuterium
isotopic contents (Table 3). Substrates converted similarly
with hydrosilylation. However, the substrate bearing a
methoxyl group as the strong electron-rich group gave only a
27% yield (4qa), which suggested that electron-deficient
groups were in favor of this conversion.
This reaction can be successfully scaled up to 2 mmol for the
example of compound 3aa (Scheme 2). Several control
experiments were carried out to shed light on the reaction

pathway. A free-radical scavenger, such as (2,2,6,6-tetrame-
thylpiperidin-1-yl)oxyl (TEMPO) or butylated hydroxytoluene
(BHT), was added to the standard conditions. As expected, the
desired conversion was outright inhibited (Scheme 3a), which
meant that a radically associated process might be involved.
The direct utilization of MePh
2
SiH as the silyl radical
precursor was also attempted (reactions b and c of Scheme
3). However, no product was detected even with additionally a
HAT catalyst or under UV irradiation, proving the unique
reactivity of silanecarboxylic acids in the photo and nickel dual
catalytic system.
On the basis of previous reports and our above
investigations, we proposed a possible mechanism, as
elucidated in Scheme 4. A carboxyl radical A as the key
species is formed by single electron transfer (SET) between
silanecarboxylic acid and the excitation of 4CzIPN, simulta-
neously accompanied by the generation of the 4CzIPN radical
anion. Then, decarboxylation of the carboxyl radical A released
a new silyl radical intermediate B, which subsequently
undergoes radical addition with 1,3-enyne to produce
propargyl radical C. Propargylic radical C can isomerize to
another resonance form, allenyl radical D, which readily
intercepts the nickel catalyst to create allenyl nickel complex E.
Finally, a protonation and another SET result in the formation
of the eventual product 3, along with the regeneration of the
nickel catalyst and the ground-state 4CzIPN.
In summary, we have disclosed a photoredox and nickel
cooperatively catalyzed hydrosilylation of 1,3-enynes, provid-
ing an efficient, concise, and modular strategy to access diverse
substituted α-silylallene derivatives with high selectivity. In this

transformation, silanecarboxylic acids as the silyl radical
precursors not only have the advantages of high stability and
easy operation but also exhibit unique reactivity in our photo/
nickel dual catalytic system. The reaction variant is particularly
synthetically valuable for the synthesis of α-silyldeuteroallenes
when performed under MeOD as the solvent. Further
investigations on the selective silicofunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes are ongoing in our laboratory.
